paragraphs: Industrial anomaly detectors often reuse features learned from ImageNet, even though recognizing natural images differs from separating normal industrial examples from defects. ADPretrain addresses both this mismatch in training goals and the difference between natural and industrial imagery. It aims to supply representations explicitly trained for anomaly detection.

The framework trains on the large industrial anomaly dataset RealIAD. Its contrastive objectives separate normal and abnormal features in two ways: by increasing the angle between them and by increasing the difference in their magnitudes. It also learns through residual features, which the authors describe as generalizable across classes, to reduce potential differences between pretraining data and downstream datasets.

The evaluation replaces the original features in five embedding-based anomaly detection methods with ADPretrain representations. Across five datasets and five backbone architectures, the experiments consistently favor the new features. This makes the contribution useful at the representation level: existing detection methods can benefit from features whose training objective and source imagery more closely match their task.
neurips-2025-adpretrain-advancing-indust.tldr: ADPretrain improves industrial anomaly detection by pretraining features to distinguish normal examples from anomalies on industrial data.

paragraphs: Optimization problems often involve objectives that conflict, so choosing a solution requires knowing which tradeoffs a decision maker prefers. This paper studies an interactive approach that learns those preferences during optimization. The goal is to concentrate on relevant solutions instead of trying to describe the entire collection of optimal tradeoffs.

The proposed method uses an ensemble of neural networks to model utility, meaning how desirable an outcome is to the decision maker. It learns from pairwise comparisons between alternatives and incorporates monotonicity: the preference model respects consistent directions of improvement. This uses structure that the authors say is common in utility functions but has received limited attention in earlier approaches.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art alternatives and robustness when utility evaluations contain noise. An ablation study identifies monotonicity as a critical contributor to the improvement. The stated findings support incorporating this preference structure into the learned utility model when guiding a search among competing objectives.
neurips-2025-bayesian-optimization-with-.tldr: A monotonic neural network ensemble learns preferences from comparisons to guide optimization toward desirable tradeoffs.

paragraphs: BrainEC-LLM adapts a pretrained language model to estimate brain effective connectivity from fMRI recordings. The task concerns directed influences between brain regions. The authors argue that existing language-model approaches to causal discovery, which repeatedly ask about pairs of variables without adapting the model, are poorly suited to the differences between brain measurements and language.

The method first separates fMRI time series into patterns at multiple scales, including shorter and longer trends. It mixes information from fine scales toward coarse scales and in the reverse direction, allowing the representation to incorporate temporal variation at different resolutions. Cross attention then connects these representations with pretrained word embeddings to align the input with the language model.

The authors present this as the first approach to fine-tune language models specifically for brain effective connectivity estimation. Evaluations on simulated and real resting-state fMRI datasets report superior performance against state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution combines model adaptation with multiscale processing, addressing both the input mismatch and the complexity of temporal relationships.
neurips-2025-brainec-llm-brain-effective.tldr: BrainEC-LLM combines multiscale fMRI processing with language-model fine-tuning to estimate directed relationships between brain regions.

paragraphs: Constrained expected improvement is a widely used strategy for optimizing a black-box objective while satisfying constraints. Despite its practical success, its theoretical convergence rate had not been established. This paper addresses that gap by bounding simple regret, which measures how far the best feasible result found remains from the optimum.

The analysis considers two mathematical settings. In the first, both the objective and constraint function belong to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In the second, both are sampled from Gaussian processes. For squared exponential kernels, the rate is t^(-1/2) times log(t)^((d+1)/2). For Matérn kernels, it is t^(-ν/(2ν+d)) times log(t)^(ν/(2ν+d)), where t counts evaluations, d is dimension, and ν controls smoothness.

The Gaussian-process setting obtains the same rates with high probability. These are guarantees under the stated function assumptions, connecting convergence to the selected kernel and problem dimension. Numerical experiments support the analysis. The contribution gives a theoretical basis for an established constrained optimization procedure.
neurips-2025-convergence-rates-of-constr.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for constrained expected improvement under kernel-space and Gaussian-process assumptions.

paragraphs: Training on more data has benefited language and image models, but graph pretraining faces an obstacle: graphs from different domains can have very different structures. UniAug explores whether a shared generative model can learn across this diversity and transfer useful structural information to downstream tasks.

The method pretrains a discrete diffusion model on thousands of graphs drawn from multiple domains. Its downstream role is to augment graph structure. Guided generation uses the pretrained model to produce structural enhancements adapted to the task being performed. This separates learning broad graph patterns from deciding how those patterns should help a particular application.

The authors report consistent performance improvements across various downstream tasks through a plug-and-play augmentation approach. They describe the work as the first demonstration, to their knowledge, of cross-domain data scaling for a graph structure augmentor. The central result is that shared structural pretraining can support task-specific graph enhancement, providing a route for heterogeneous graph data to contribute to downstream performance.
neurips-2025-cross-domain-graph-data-sca.tldr: UniAug learns graph structure across domains with diffusion pretraining and uses guided augmentation to improve downstream tasks.

paragraphs: A control algorithm's performance in production depends on how its parameters and logic are adjusted to the situation. Evaluations using default or ideal configurations can overlook this capacity for improvement. Crucible studies that capacity directly, calling it tuning potential and making it an explicit target of algorithm evaluation.

Crucible uses an LLM-driven agent to simulate expert tuning at multiple levels. Alongside this tuning process, the authors introduce a formal metric for quantifying tuning potential. The approach therefore connects an automated way of exploring adjustments with a way of comparing how much different algorithms can benefit from them.

The paper evaluates Crucible across case studies ranging from classical control problems to complex computer systems, and validates its findings in a real deployment. The experiments indicate that it systematically measures the space available for tuning across algorithms. The authors also report performance improvements arising from this perspective, positioning tuning potential as an additional consideration in algorithm analysis and design.
neurips-2025-crucible-quantifying-the-po.tldr: Crucible uses an LLM agent and a formal metric to assess how much control algorithms can improve through tuning.

paragraphs: DiCo investigates whether convolutional networks can provide an efficient foundation for diffusion-based image generation. The motivation comes from analyzing pretrained diffusion transformers: their global attention often captures predominantly local patterns. That observation suggests an opportunity to use convolution, but simply replacing attention with convolution reduces performance.

The authors attribute this gap to greater redundancy among convolutional feature channels. They introduce a compact channel attention mechanism that encourages more diverse channels to become active. The resulting DiCo family uses standard convolutional-network modules while addressing the loss of feature diversity identified in the direct replacement approach.

For class-conditioned ImageNet generation, DiCo-XL reports FID scores of 2.05 at 256×256 resolution and 2.53 at 512×512. Its corresponding speedups over DiT-XL/2 are 2.7× and 3.1×. Experiments on MS-COCO also show potential for text-to-image generation. These findings support convolution as a competitive building block when its channel redundancy is addressed, rather than treating the initial performance drop as decisive.
neurips-2025-dico-revitalizing-convnets-.tldr: DiCo improves channel diversity in convolutional diffusion models, achieving strong image generation with reported speedups over a diffusion transformer.

paragraphs: Time-series imputation fills gaps in partially observed data. Diffusion models have performed well at this task, but their empirical success leaves theoretical questions about how they capture relationships between observed and missing values. This paper studies conditional diffusion transformers, focusing on data requirements and uncertainty about the values being filled in.

The authors develop an approximation theory for conditional score functions represented by transformers. This provides the basis for statistical sample-complexity bounds, which describe the amount of data needed for estimation. They also use the analysis to construct tight confidence regions for missing values, extending the treatment beyond producing a single completed series.

A key finding is that the arrangement of missing entries substantially affects imputation efficiency and accuracy. Simulations validate the theoretical insights, and the authors propose training with a mixture of masking patterns to improve performance. The work therefore connects mathematical analysis to a training choice: how missingness is represented during learning matters for reconstructing incomplete time series.
neurips-2025-diffusion-transformers-for-.tldr: The paper derives data-efficiency and uncertainty results for diffusion-transformer imputation and shows that missing-value patterns matter.

paragraphs: Hybrid language models combine attention with state space models, creating a compression problem that differs from shrinking attention-only architectures. This paper develops a compression recipe that accounts for the organization of Mamba layers. Its central concern is retaining the structure that lets state space blocks model sequences while reducing model size.

The proposed group-aware pruning method removes components in a way designed to preserve that structure. It is combined with pruning of feed-forward networks, embedding dimensions, and whole layers. Knowledge distillation then retrains the compressed model using guidance from a larger model, bringing these separate compression choices into one workflow.

Using this recipe, the authors reduce Nemotron-H from eight billion to four billion parameters. They report using up to 40 times fewer training tokens than similarly sized models. The resulting model exceeds the accuracy of similarly sized alternatives while delivering approximately twice the inference throughput. The findings show a favorable measured combination of training cost, accuracy, and runtime for this hybrid-model compression approach.
neurips-2025-efficient-hybrid-language-m.tldr: Structure-aware pruning and distillation compress Nemotron-H from 8B to 4B parameters with strong reported accuracy and inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers generate coherent motion, raising a question about their internal representations: where do they encode which locations correspond across frames? DiffTrack introduces a quantitative framework for examining these temporal relationships. It studies components of the models' full three-dimensional attention, including representations, layers, and denoising timesteps.

The framework builds a dataset of prompt-generated videos with pseudo ground-truth tracking annotations and introduces evaluation metrics for correspondence analysis. The authors find that query-key similarity supports temporal matching in particular layers, rather than uniformly throughout the network. This matching also becomes more prominent as denoising proceeds, linking correspondence formation to the generation process.

The paper applies these findings to zero-shot point tracking and reports state-of-the-art performance against existing vision foundation models and self-supervised video models. It also introduces guidance that improves the temporal consistency of generated videos without further training. The contribution connects analysis of internal attention with practical uses for tracking and motion-aware generation.
neurips-2025-emergent-temporal-correspon.tldr: DiffTrack identifies temporal matching inside video diffusion transformers and applies it to point tracking and more consistent video generation.

paragraphs: Low-bit floating-point arithmetic can accelerate training, but its benefits depend on the operations being performed. FALQON examines why FP8 is less helpful for low-rank adaptation, or LoRA. The small matrices used by LoRA leave less computation over which to spread the overhead of quantization, reducing the expected speed benefit.

The framework merges LoRA adapters directly into an FP8-quantized backbone during fine-tuning. This removes quantization overhead associated with separate adapter computation paths. The authors also reformulate the forward and backward computations and introduce a row-wise proxy update mechanism to incorporate substantial updates efficiently into the quantized backbone.

Experiments report approximately threefold training acceleration over existing quantized LoRA methods at a similar level of accuracy. The end-to-end FP8 workflow also avoids a separate post-training quantization step. The contribution is therefore a redesign of how adaptation interacts with quantized computation, addressing overhead that can otherwise prevent low-bit hardware support from translating into faster fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-falqon-accelerating-lora-fi.tldr: FALQON merges LoRA adapters into an FP8 backbone during fine-tuning, reporting roughly threefold faster training at similar accuracy.

paragraphs: Video language models spend substantial computation processing video tokens that contain overlapping information. FastVID studies this redundancy through both temporal context and visual context. Its goal is to remove unnecessary tokens while retaining the information needed to understand what appears in a video and how it changes over time.

The method dynamically divides a video into segments that remain in temporal order. It then uses density-based token pruning to preserve essential spatial and temporal information. Combining segmentation with pruning addresses the structure of video redundancy, rather than treating every token as an isolated candidate for removal.

Evaluations cover short and long videos across several leading video language models. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, FastVID removes 90.3% of video tokens, brings FLOPs down to 8.3% of the original amount, and accelerates prefilling by 7.1× while retaining 98.0% of original accuracy. These results demonstrate a substantial measured efficiency gain, with the reported speedup specifically applying to the prefilling stage.
neurips-2025-fastvid-dynamic-density-pru.tldr: FastVID prunes redundant video tokens while preserving temporal structure, substantially accelerating prefilling with limited measured accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Scaling laws turn measurements from trained models into prescriptions about how to scale future models. Those prescriptions are often fitted using model families with a narrow set of fixed hyperparameters. Gemstones examines how expanding the architectural and training choices changes the conclusions that such fits produce.

The main artifact is an open-source dataset containing more than 4,000 transformer checkpoints, with models reaching two billion parameters. The suite varies architectural shape and includes ablations of learning rate and cooldown. This variety supports questions that a narrowly configured model family cannot explore as directly, including the relationship between network width and depth.

Analysis of the suite finds that scaling prescriptions can be highly sensitive to experimental design and to the particular checkpoints included in fitting. The finding makes the selection of training runs part of interpreting a scaling result. Gemstones contributes both evidence for this sensitivity and a broader collection of checkpoints for studying how architectural and hyperparameter choices affect scaling conclusions.
neurips-2025-gemstones-a-model-suite-for.tldr: Gemstones provides over 4,000 diverse transformer checkpoints and shows that scaling-law prescriptions can depend strongly on experimental design.

paragraphs: HiPoNet analyzes high-dimensional point clouds, motivated by single-cell datasets whose measurements extend far beyond three-dimensional coordinates. It also addresses cohorts containing a separate dataset for each patient. The network supports classification, regression, and representation learning for entire point clouds, rather than focusing only on individual points.

Instead of building one nearest-neighbor graph, HiPoNet constructs multiple simplicial complexes, which represent higher-order relationships among points. Each view uses a different reweighting of features. Simplicial wavelet transforms then extract patterns at multiple scales, capturing local and global topology. In biological data, these different views offer the possibility of separating distinct cellular processes.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that the framework preserves geometric and topological information. Experiments on single-cell data show better performance than other point-cloud and graph-based models. The method is also applied to spatial transcriptomics, with spatial coordinates serving as one view. Its contribution is a trainable way to combine multiple structural perspectives on high-dimensional datasets.
neurips-2025-hiponet-a-multi-view-simpli.tldr: HiPoNet combines multiple higher-order structural views to learn from high-dimensional point clouds and single-cell datasets.

paragraphs: When participants nominate one another for selection, they may manipulate their nominations to improve their own prospects. Impartial mechanisms remove this incentive by making each participant's selection independent of the nominations that participant submits. This paper asks how predictions about the most-nominated participants can improve selection while preserving impartiality.

The analysis separates consistency, or performance when predictions are correct, from robustness, or performance when predictions are wrong. When selecting up to k participants and allowing each to nominate any number of others, the proposed mechanism achieves consistency 1−O(1/k) and robustness 1−1/e−O(1/k). These bounds quantify the benefit of accurate predictions alongside protection against inaccurate ones.

For selecting a single participant when everyone makes one nomination, the authors prove that perfect consistency can coexist with one-half robustness. Comparing these guarantees with prior results shows that asymptotically optimal consistency can require little or no robustness sacrifice. The contribution is a set of theoretical guarantees for using predictive information without abandoning the incentive protection of impartial selection.
neurips-2025-impartial-selection-with-pr.tldr: Prediction-assisted impartial selection can improve outcomes when predictions are correct while retaining strong guarantees when they are wrong.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data without rebuilding a language model from scratch. This paper identifies a vulnerability in fine-tuning-based unlearning: a manipulated forgetting request can cause damage to ordinary model use. The problem arises when the effect of forgetting spreads beyond its intended scope.

The authors demonstrate a Stealthy Attack that strengthens associations between common benign tokens and the signals a model learns to forget. As a result, ordinary prompts containing those tokens can trigger hallucinations or apparent ignorance associated with unlearning. This connects unintended utility loss to both weak control over forgetting scope and difficulty separating benign content from forgetting signals.

The proposed remedy, Scope-aware Unlearning, adds a scope term to the training objective to encourage more localized forgetting. It requires no additional data processing and fits into existing fine-tuning workflows. Experiments validate the attack and show that the remedy significantly improves robustness against it, making control of unlearning's reach a concrete design concern.
neurips-2025-keeping-an-eye-on-llm-unlea.tldr: Manipulated forgetting requests can harm ordinary language-model use; Scope-aware Unlearning improves robustness by encouraging localized forgetting.

paragraphs: Greedy Equivalence Search learns causal graph structure from observational data by comparing scores. In the infinite-sample limit, it identifies a class of graphs that observational data cannot distinguish. Less Greedy Equivalence Search modifies this procedure to improve computational cost and finite-sample accuracy while retaining its theoretical recovery guarantees.

The change concerns which edges the search inserts. Rather than always taking the highest-scoring insertion, LGES avoids connecting variables when the score indicates some conditional independence between them. It can also use prior knowledge to guide the search and revise that knowledge when the data contradict it. Interventional data can further refine the learned equivalence class.

The authors prove recovery of the true equivalence class in the sample limit even with misspecified prior knowledge. Experiments report up to a tenfold speedup and substantially lower structural error relative to GES, together with advantages over other baselines. The result shows how a more selective search can improve practical behavior without giving up the stated asymptotic guarantee.
neurips-2025-less-greedy-equivalence-sea.tldr: LGES makes causal graph search more selective, improving measured speed and accuracy while preserving sample-limit recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Unstructured pruning compresses a language model by removing individual weight parameters. A central challenge is deciding where those removals should occur. Existing methods often prune one layer at a time to manage the scale of the problem, but their layer-level sparsity choices can produce a suboptimal allocation for the model as a whole.

Lua-LLM treats sparsity allocation as a learning problem across the model. It allows flexible decisions both between layers and within each layer. A soft Top-K operator approximates the process of choosing weights by importance, enabling efficient learning of binary masks that determine which parameters remain active.

Experiments on the LLaMA and OPT model families report significant performance improvements over existing methods. The contribution is therefore broader than choosing a pruning amount for each layer: it learns a more detailed distribution of retained weights. This addresses the mismatch between convenient layer-by-layer compression decisions and the objective of preserving performance across the entire model.
neurips-2025-lua-llm-learning-unstructur.tldr: Lua-LLM learns where to prune weights across and within layers, improving reported performance over existing pruning methods.

paragraphs: A multimodal model can give an incorrect answer because it misreads an image or because it reasons incorrectly about an image it understood. MIRAGE separates these sources of failure by constructing questions where image perception is correct but reasoning errors remain. This makes reasoning-induced hallucination a more direct target of evaluation.

The benchmark evaluates accuracy, factuality, and an LLM-based hallucination score. Its analysis finds strong relationships between question types and particular hallucination patterns. Complex spatial relationships, including geometric patterns across images, expose systematic reasoning failures. These findings identify specific kinds of reasoning that require attention even when visual recognition succeeds.

The paper also introduces Logos, combining curriculum reinforcement fine-tuning with collaborative hint inference. The training component encourages logically consistent reasoning through stepwise reductions in learning difficulty, while hints reduce inference complexity. Logos establishes a benchmark baseline and reduces logical hallucinations in the original base models. Together, the benchmark and method connect diagnosis of reasoning failures with a targeted attempt to reduce them.
neurips-2025-mirage-assessing-hallucinat.tldr: MIRAGE isolates reasoning hallucinations after correct image perception, while Logos reduces them through curriculum training and collaborative hints.

paragraphs: Large tables require a model to locate individual cells reliably before more complex analysis can be trusted. NeedleInATable tests this basic capability directly. Existing long-context benchmarks emphasize unstructured text, while many table benchmarks emphasize higher-level reasoning, leaving precise cell retrieval in long structured inputs less examined.

The benchmark treats each cell as a target to retrieve, using either its location or a lookup question. Evaluations of language models and multimodal language models reveal a substantial gap between performance on familiar downstream table tasks and this simpler retrieval task. The authors suggest that strong downstream scores may sometimes reflect dataset-specific correlations or shortcuts rather than robust table understanding.

Training with synthesized NeedleInATable examples improves performance both on the benchmark itself and on downstream table tasks. This result supports the importance of fine-grained cell access as a useful capability for broader table processing. The contribution is a focused test and training resource that makes an underlying component of long-context table understanding directly measurable.
neurips-2025-needleinatable-exploring-lo.tldr: NeedleInATable exposes weaknesses in retrieving cells from long tables and shows that targeted training can improve broader table tasks.

paragraphs: Agnostic learning allows the best classifier in a chosen hypothesis class to make mistakes. This paper studies how learning difficulty changes when that best achievable error, τ, is small. Standard worst-case guarantees can obscure this easier regime, motivating bounds that explicitly depend on τ as well as sample size and class complexity.

The authors construct a computationally efficient learner using carefully combined empirical-risk-minimization classifiers. With m samples, VC dimension d, and failure probability δ, its error is bounded by cτ plus terms of order sqrt(τ(d+log(1/δ))/m) and (d+log(1/δ))/m, where c is at most 2.1. The bound achieves the optimal rate when τ is O(d/m).

This resolves the question of whether the regime near τ=d/m requires a larger lower bound. The result also advances questions about computational efficiency and aggregation of empirical-risk-minimization classifiers. Reducing the multiplier on τ from 2.1 to 1 remains open; the authors identify that refinement as necessary to completely settle the broader learning-complexity question.
neurips-2025-on-agnostic-pac-learning-in.tldr: An efficient aggregation-based learner achieves optimal error rates in the small-error regime, while a sharper leading constant remains open.

paragraphs: In a sequence model, a prediction can depend on both a feature's value and its position. Attribution methods that hold ordering fixed can mix these influences together. OrdShap addresses this ambiguity by asking how the prediction changes when feature positions are permuted, making position itself part of the explanation.

The method is designed for explaining sequential black-box models after training. It separates the contribution of feature values from the contribution of their placement in the sequence. The authors establish a connection to Sanchez-Bergantiños values from game theory, providing a theoretical foundation for assigning importance when ordering affects the outcome.

Experiments on health, natural-language, and synthetic datasets demonstrate the method's ability to capture both value and position attributions. This matters because an explanation of which inputs are important can remain incomplete when it ignores where they occur. OrdShap adds that positional perspective, helping describe how a sequence model uses its inputs rather than collapsing content and ordering into a single attribution.
neurips-2025-ordshap-feature-position-im.tldr: OrdShap separates the influence of feature values from their sequence positions when explaining black-box predictions.

paragraphs: RAD brings external medical knowledge directly into multimodal diagnostic tasks. Its motivation is that knowledge stored implicitly in model parameters may not supply the specific guidance a downstream task requires. The framework therefore retrieves and refines disease-focused knowledge from multiple medical sources as part of the diagnostic approach.

Two mechanisms connect that knowledge to the model. A guideline-enhanced contrastive loss brings multimodal features into alignment with guideline representations. A dual transformer decoder uses guidelines as queries to guide the combination of modalities. Together, these components connect knowledge acquisition, feature extraction, and decision-making around clinical guidance.

The authors also introduce quantitative interpretability criteria covering image and text perspectives. Across four datasets involving different anatomies, RAD achieves reported state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates generalizability. The model focuses more precisely on abnormal image regions and important indicators. These findings support the framework's goal of making diagnostic predictions more closely connected to relevant guidance and observable evidence in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-rad-towards-trustworthy-ret.tldr: RAD retrieves medical guidance to shape multimodal diagnosis, improving reported performance and attention to relevant diagnostic evidence.

paragraphs: Many theoretical analyses of recurrent networks assume Gaussian connection weights, while evidence about brain synapses motivates heavier-tailed distributions. This paper studies random networks with Lévy alpha-stable weights. It focuses on how finite network size changes the transition between a quiet state and chaotic activity.

Infinite-system mean-field theory predicts that the quiet state is always unstable. The finite-size analysis instead finds a sharp transition and predicts the gain at which it occurs, with simulations validating the prediction. Compared with Gaussian networks, finite heavy-tailed networks remain near the edge of chaos over a broader range of gain values.

That broader transition region comes with a tradeoff. Heavier tails lower the attractor's Lyapunov dimension, indicating that the activity has fewer effective dimensions. The findings connect greater robustness of near-chaotic dynamics with reduced richness of high-dimensional activity. By analyzing finite networks directly, the paper provides a framework for studying realistically sized circuits where the infinite-system prediction does not capture the transition.
neurips-2025-slow-transition-to-low-dime.tldr: Finite heavy-tailed recurrent networks have a broader edge-of-chaos regime, accompanied by lower-dimensional chaotic activity.

paragraphs: Most language-model agents collaborate by exchanging language or token embeddings. This paper proposes communication through underlying latent representations, termed thoughts. It formalizes agent states as observations generated by an unknown function of hidden variables, making the shared information behind those states the object to recover and communicate.

Within the paper's nonparametric latent-variable setting, the authors prove that shared and private thoughts between pairs of agents are identifiable without auxiliary information. They also provide guarantees for recovering the global sharing structure: which agents share which latent thoughts and how those relationships fit together. These results guide a framework that extracts thoughts and assigns relevant ones, together with sharing patterns, to agents.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks support the theory and demonstrate collaborative advantages. The formulation also extends beyond language models to other modalities generated from hidden processes. The contribution links theoretical recovery of shared latent information with a communication framework, giving agents a way to exchange inferred underlying structure alongside its relationships across participants.
neurips-2025-thought-communication-in-mu.tldr: The paper develops latent-variable theory and a framework for agents to collaborate by communicating recovered shared representations.
